title: Linked Speech / Legato
learningGoals: Keep ordinary sound closures and pauses

sections.heading: Welcome and what we will explore
sections.narration:
Welcome. Today we are exploring Linked Speech / Legato. Each word feels like another separate start, and the effort of restarting crowds a short request.

We will hear a short connected phrase, separate connection from speed, and keep ordinary sound closures and pauses. First I will explain the distinction. Then you will see and hear a demonstration, try a few short phrases, and notice your own experience. We will finish with a short prepared rehearsal and an everyday next step. You can pause or ask a question at any point. A small comfortable experiment is enough.

sections.heading: What this tool means
sections.narration:
Legato means connected. Here it describes the movement of a short spoken phrase rather than an instruction to make every sound continuous. Connection and speed are different: a connected phrase may be ordinary in pace or a little slower. A normal closure on a sound still belongs in the message.

Linked speech lets a short phrase move as a connected message. You do not need to restart the voice and effort before each word. This can be explored at different speeds; connection and pace are separate features. Normal sound closures and phrase boundaries still belong in speech. Keep the phrase short enough to say comfortably.

Notice the distinction: Connection does not remove voiceless sounds, normal closures or the need to breathe. It can be explored at more than one pace. You are choosing one feature for this learning experience, rather than inspecting every aspect of speech. We will use short familiar messages so there is room to notice that feature.

sections.heading: Watch and listen
sections.narration:
Watch the demonstration before trying. We will use this message: I would like to know more. First listen to the models and notice the feature being compared. The labels on screen identify each version. You can replay either model without copying an uncomfortable contrast.

Now listen once more for the message itself. Connection between words, physical effort and whether the meaning remains clear. This is an invitation to compare your experience, not a demand to match the model exactly. When you are ready, move to a short guided attempt.

sections.heading: Try the three small steps
sections.narration:
Let us try this in small steps. First: Choose a short phrase with one clear meaning. Next: Listen for connections rather than equal beats. Then: Try the phrase, then add a natural pause before another idea.

Use these familiar phrases one at a time: I would like to know more. Thank you for taking the time. Let us look at the next step. Stop between attempts when you want to. You can listen to a model again, record a short attempt, or leave this part to return later. Keep attention on this one chosen feature; you do not need to check every sound. If the attempt becomes effortful, stop and return to comfortable ordinary speaking.

sections.heading: Compare and check
sections.narration:
Consider what this tool is asking you to explore. What does linked speech require? You can select an answer and read or hear the explanation. It is a check of the idea, not a test of how you sound.

After the check, notice one observation from your attempt: Connection between words, physical effort and whether the meaning remains clear. It is possible for a movement to feel different while the message still takes effort, or for you to be unsure what changed. You can record that uncertainty without repeating until you obtain a preferred result.

sections.heading: From a phrase to your own message
sections.narration:
Choose a short message you actually want to share. You might use one of the phrases we have practised and add one useful detail in your own words. Give yourself one small cue from the demonstration, then let the message continue. There is no need to increase the amount of the technique to make the attempt count.

After speaking, ask what you noticed about the chosen feature and about the message. You can keep a small useful change, adjust it, or leave the result open. Try another short message only if it serves your learning today.

sections.heading: Your observation and next step
sections.narration:
Before finishing, save one observation. Here is the feature we explored: Connection between words, physical effort and whether the meaning remains clear. Something may have changed, things may have felt much the same, or you may be unsure. Your observation belongs to this attempt and setting.

In focused practice, you can deliberately explore this one feature. In conversation, give most of your attention to the message and the other person. A familiar support can be available if it helps; it does not need to become a checklist you monitor throughout the exchange.

Choose one manageable situation in which you would like to speak. You can plan a small practice, have a conversation, revisit the demonstration, or finish here. Save what you would keep, change or leave open.
